fragments.text: In 1994, rangers at a game reserve in
South Africa started finding dead
rhinos, [music]
poachers. Obviously, there was no second
theory except the horn was still
attached. Whoever killed this rhino had
left behind the only part of it worth
money. Then they found the next body and
the next about one a month every month.
And on every carcass the same impossible
wounds, deep punctures driven down into
the back and shoulders from above,
broken ribs. One animal had internal
injuries that could only have come from
something enormous kneeling on top of
it. And around every kill site, the same
signature. Flattened brush, uprooted
trees, and pressed into the dirt.
Footprints the size of dinner plates.
Elephant tracks. This is Palanesburg.
It's the cleanest answer anyone has ever
gotten to a much older question. Why the
young need the old? The tracks made no
sense because elephants do not kill
rhinos. The two species have shared a
continent for millions of years, mostly
by ignoring each other. In the rare
recorded cases where an elephant killed
one, it was a mother defending her calf
at a water hole. This was different.
Some of the victims had been chased down
first, attacked again and again.
Whatever was doing this was not
defending anything. It was hunting. In
1979, South Africa took a ring of old
volcanic hills covered in worn out
farmland and decided to turn it back
into wild Africa. Around 6,000 animals
were trucked in. an entire ecosystem
delivered by road. And in 1980, the
elephants arrived, 18 of them, every
single one a child. Orphans between 4
and 6 years old. Not one adult came with
them. And the reason why is the dark
heart of this story. The orphans came
from Krueger National Park. Krueger had
the opposite problem from almost every
other park in Africa. Fenced in and
protected from poaching, it had too many
elephants. So from 1967 onward, it did
what was considered responsible wildlife
management at the time. Every year it
called them. A helicopter would come in
low over a herd and a marksman would
shoot the matriarch first, the oldest
female, the one carrying the family's
entire memory. Where the water is in a
drought year, which things are
dangerous, how worried to be. When she
is calm, everyone is calm. And when she
falls, nobody runs. Elephants don't
abandon their dead. The family gathers
around her body and tries to lift her
back up. So the shooters would work
through them where they stood one by one
until the whole herd was down. The logic
was that this was the humane version.
Leaving survivors in a species that
remembers everything was considered
cruer than erasing the whole unit at
once. More than 14,000 elephants were
killed this way over three decades. But
the youngest calves were spared. Not out
of mercy exactly. They were spared
because they were the only ones small
enough to move. No crane in existence
could transport a six-tonon adult. a
calf you could load. So the calves stood
by while their entire families were
shot. Then they were rounded up, put on
trucks, and sold or donated to parks
that wanted elephants again. Parks like
Palanisburg. Nobody involved was a
villain. The officials knew the orphans
might struggle, [music] but the
alternative was shooting them, too.
Saving the children was the good option,
and so a brand new park received 18
traumatized orphans, tipped them out
into the bush, and left them to raise
themselves. A wild calf grows up inside
a moving wall of adults. Every hour of
its childhood, a demonstration of what
an elephant is supposed to be. At
Palanesburg, the wall was made of other
children. Within 2 years, the managers
could tell something was off. The
youngsters were nervous, unruly,
aggressive. [music] So, in 1982, the
park brought in two adult females,
hoping a little supervision would settle
them down. Two mothers for a population
of children that would eventually grow
to around 70. And the deliveries kept
coming. More calls, more orphans. Year
after year until 1993, the park was full
of elephants and empty of adults. The
oldest elephants those orphans had ever
known were each other. Through the
1980s, they grew up and the park started
seeing behavior never documented in
elephants anywhere. Safari vehicles got
mock charged, then actually charged.
Tourists were chased. In 1993, one of
the young bulls killed a tourist. A
professional hunter was sent in to
destroy him. The elephant killed him,
too, before he could take the shot. And
the following year, the rhinos started
dying. In a normal year, Palanisburg
lost a rhino to natural causes every 2
or 3 months. In the 3 months after April
1994, 10 rhinos died violently. Five
more were found wounded. By the end of
the year, the count was 20. The white
rhino had been down to a few dozen
animals a century earlier, nursed back
one calf at a time. Now, something
inside a protected reserve was killing
them faster than poachers ever had. The
rangers responded the way detectives
respond to a serial case. They
photographed every kill site and logged
every set of tracks. When a helicopter
crew caught an attack in progress,
[music] they drove the elephant off and
airlifted the wounded rhino out of the
park. It survived. The attacker got
away. Scouts then found three teenage
bulls loitering near the scene. The
evidence was circumstantial and the park
knew it. They shot all three anyway. The
killings stopped. Then in 1996, 20 more
rhinos died. The park had shot the wrong
elephants, or at least not the only
ones. So, they ran a two-year
surveillance operation on their own
animals. Rangers marked suspects with
paint from helicopters. Researchers
built an identicate file on every male
in the park. Ear notches, tusk shapes,
scars. They were effectively compiling
wrap sheets and they gave their suspects
names. One young bull, a regular near
the death scenes, they called Tom Thumb.
In 1997, they finally caught a young
male in the act. in daylight, [music]
killing a white rhino. By now, there
were two competing explanations. The
first was trauma. These animals had
watched their families die, and a
childhood like that, some argued, could
only end in violence. The park's
ecologists weren't convinced. Trauma
might explain the anger. It couldn't
explain the timing because the attacks
came in clusters, and the clusters had a
rhythm. When the surveillance data came
together, the rhythm was the answer.
Every attacker was male. Every attacker
was one of the orphans, now in his late
teens or early 20s. And every single one
of them at the time of the attacks was
in must. Must is a hormonal state adult
bulls cycle through. Testosterone climbs
to many times its normal level. The
glands on the sides of the head swell
and stream an oily fluid. The bull
dribbles urine constantly, barely eats,
and becomes for a while the most
aggressive version of himself. It's
normal. It's how bulls compete to breed,
but it's meant to arrive late and arrive
small. In a wild herd, a male leaves his
family in his early teens and joins bull
society. Loose bands of males anchored
by giants in their 40s and 50s. He
starts at the bottom and his body knows
it. A bull hits his first musth around
his late 20s and at first it lasts only
days [music] because when he runs into a
real bull, his system registers that
he's outranked and the state can simply
switch off. Older males act as a ceiling
on younger ones just by existing. The
Pilinesberg males were entering must
around 18, a decade too early. And
instead of days, it was lasting months,
3 months, 5 months. Young bodies flooded
with fight hormones on a hair trigger
for close to half the year. In a normal
population, an older bull would have
shut that down almost on contact.
Palanisburg didn't contain a single one.
Bull society didn't exist here. Neither
did the ceiling. The famous killer
animals of history almost always turned
out to have something broken in their
bodies. A shattered jaw, a crippled
foot. The Pylonberg males were studied
from every angle and their bodies were
perfect. The wound was in their
biography. The rhinos were the collision
point. The young males had grown up
loosely mixed in with them, possibly
because nothing had ever taught them
where elephants end and other species
[music] begin. When the hormones hit,
the nearest thing they had to arrival
was a two-tonon animal that couldn't
outrank them and couldn't escape them.
By the time it was over, researchers
estimated the elephants had killed as
many as 49 rhinos. Roughly 1 in 10 of
the rhinos in the park. Several of the
orphans had been shot for it. Shooting
their way out was the obvious next step,
and Palanesburg refused to take it.
Because by now, the park's field
ecologist, Gus Van Djk, and his
colleagues had arrived at a different
diagnosis. The [music] park didn't have
bad elephants. The park was missing
elephants. The violence wasn't a
property of the animals. It was a
property of the world they'd been
handed. So, the park proposed something
nobody had ever done. Import the missing
adults. [music] For 20 years, that had
been physically impossible. It was the
entire reason the orphans existed. But
by the late 1990s, engineers had built
reinforced trucks and cranes that could
handle six tons of living resisting
animal. For the first time in history, a
full-grown bull elephant could be moved.
In early 1998 in Krueger, they captured
six of them, adult bulls, 25 to 35 years
old, each one bigger than anything the
orphans had ever seen. They were hauled
across the country, held for 3 days in
an enclosure to learn what an electric
fence was, and [music] released. Nobody
trained them. Nobody managed what
happened next. Six older bulls walked
out into the park and simply began
existing. Within a year, every elephant
in Palanesburg had crossed paths with
them. Young males in must swaggered up
to challenge the newcomers and
discovered for the first time in their
lives what it feels like to be
outranked. Researchers began noticing
fresh puncture wounds just above the
young bull's tails. The best
explanation, the older males were
putting them in their place, tusk
[music] first. The teenagers stopped
wandering alone and started shadowing
the big bulls the way they should have
been doing since they were 12 and then
their body chemistry reorganized itself.
Must that had been arriving at 18 was
delayed. must that had been running for
months collapsed in some cases within
minutes of meeting a bigger bull. The
park called it a total turnaround. Van
Dick compared it to a gang of teenagers
who had been running wild, suddenly
finding their fathers standing in the
room. The rhino killings didn't slow
down. They stopped. [music] In the years
after the bulls arrived, Pilannesburg
did not lose a single rhino to an
elephant. Even Tom Thumb left the rhinos
alone. The biologist Rob Slatau Van Dyk
and their colleagues published the
finding in Nature. The title was six
words long. Older bull elephants control
young males. Strip everything else away.
And this is what the accident
demonstrated. A society is not food,
space, [music] and safety. The orphans
had all three. A society has an
architecture. And the top layer of that
architecture does work that is invisible
until it's gone. The presence of the old
sets the clock on the young. It decides
when aggression arrives, how long it
stays, and how far it's allowed to go.
None of that gets taught. It's
transmitted by standing there. remove
the layer and nothing happens at first.
The children are fed, they grow, the
bill arrives 15 years later when
adolescence walks into a world with
nothing above it. Put the layer back and
the whole system reeregulates within a
season. And one detail makes the finding
airtight. The bulls healed nothing.
Decades later, researchers went back and
tested the Pilinisburg orphans and the
damage was still in them. They couldn't
judge threats the way normal elephant
families do. The young need somewhere to
look when they [music] don't know what
to be. Elephants got the controlled
experiment. Humans never will. Nobody
gets to truck six father figures into a
broken neighborhood and publish the
result. So, nobody can say for certain
how much of this story is really about
elephants. The most violent elephants
ever documented, animals with kill
counts, animals that hunted, went back
to being ordinary elephants within a
single season. Nothing about them had
